newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico sees record crude output even in price fall.
newsitem.headline: Mexico sees record crude output even in price fall.

text.p: Mexico crude output in February peaked at five-year record levels even as oil prices continued to fall from post-Gulf War highs.

Mexico's state oil and gas monopoly Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex) said it flirted with the three million barrels per day (bpd) barrier last topped in 1982, with February average production of 2.968 million barrels per day (bpd).
As part of a greater program to step up production efforts, Pemex has projected average 1997 output of 3.083 million bpd, a 7.9 percent increase from 2.858 million the year before.

"Pemex last exceeded output of three million (bpd) in 1982 at the tail end of the oil boom. There's always a lag time between the well in the ground and when oil starts flowing," Mexico energy consultant George Baker told Reuters.
Analysts said higher international crude prices encouraged the company to boost exploration and production for 1997, as Pemex almost doubled its E&P budget to $4.069 billion.
"When prices go up, companies dedicate more resources to production and more expensive exploration methods," Baker said.
But world crude prices have slowly sank from when Mexico's average export prices per barrel of crude peaked in October at $22.20, its highest level in at least five years.
Pemex's heavy crude Maya sold at about $20.56 per barrel, light Isthmus sold at $22.87 and extra-light Olmeca sold for $24.74 for the month.
In past months crude prices have fallen to March averages of $14.48 per barrel of Maya, $17.78 for Isthmus and $19.79 for Olmeca.

Windfall from the leap in oil prices brought much needed capital to Pemex, and in turn the Mexican government, which claims more than two-thirds of Pemex revenue. The company's pre-tax revenue jumped 32 percent in 1996 to $21.07 million.
"The rest of the economy is not doing very well and one place where the government can get more international profit and better foreign exchange is in the oil sector," Baker added.
The drop in crude prices may throw a wrench in the government's hopes for even greater revenues, but it does follow with Pemex's conservative expectations.

Even with higher crude production, Pemex chairman Adrian Lajous said last year that 1997 export revenue expectations would reflect an average oil price estimate of $14.50 per barrel, and drop to $9.02 billion from about $10.705 billion in 1996.

"Lower prices this year will not make budgets as comfortable," Petroleum Industry Research Foundation vice-president Cheryl Trench said, adding Pemex's growth plans are encouraging and should improve Gulf of Campeche maintenance.

Analysts think Pemex could increase production even more and have criticized Pemex for not sufficiently exploiting its petroleum reserves potential. Critics point to the example of its more aggressive competitor, Petroleos de Venezuela, (PdVSA).

PdVSA surpassed Pemex's output with over three million bpd in crude production in 1996, aided by a system of private company contracting which Pemex prohibits. The Venezuelan state oil company plans to increase production capacity to 3.71 million bpd this year and 6.2 million bpd by 2006.
